content.text:
1. Make a guess before the next step: can you draw a perfect circle freehand, with no help at all? Try one on paper.
2. Now trace a bangle and put the two next to each other. The freehand one wobbles, the traced one is round.
3. A ruler draws straight lines and a compass draws round curves. With these two tools we can build faces, waves, houses, squares and rectangles exactly.

media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 8 'Playing with Constructions' (The Compass and Circles). Fix the compass point. Swing the pencil. Draw a circle. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Compass Circle Maker. Fix the compass point. Swing the pencil. Draw a circle. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: A compass keeps one distance fixed, so every point it draws is the same distance, the radius, from the centre; the radius is half of the width across.
tool_config.title: Compass Circle Maker
tool_config.screen: A sheet with a ruler along the bottom; a compass whose opening is set against the ruler; a centre point that can be dragged; a pencil that sweeps round; a radius read-out and a width-across read-out.
feedback: Setting the opening from the end of the ruler instead of its zero mark shows the true opening beside the one typed, so the slip is seen.
Typing the width across as the radius shows the radius as half of that width.
A solved card shows the centre, the radius line and the finished circle.
challenges: Radius 3 cm: how wide is the circle across? (6 cm)
A circle 10 cm across: what radius do you set? (5 cm)
Two circles of radius 2 cm touch: how far apart are the centres? (4 cm)
Two circles share a centre, radii 2 cm and 4 cm: how wide is the gap between them? (2 cm)
Two circles of radius 3 cm overlap with centres 4 cm apart: is the centre of one inside the other? (yes)
Radius 2.5 cm: how wide across? (5 cm)

hint_ladder.text: What does the compass opening stand for?
The opening is the radius, and the width across is two radii.
Read the radius or the width in the card and halve or double it.

Set the compass opening against the ruler and fix the centre.

content.text:
Worked example: Look at five artwork pictures: two circles of the same size side by side and touching; two circles one inside the other with the same centre (the inner one about half the size of the outer); three equal circles in a row, each overlapping the next; a mouse face (one big circle for the face, two smaller circles for the ears, two small circles with dots for the eyes, a dot for the nose and a short line for the mouth); and two lines crossing like an X with a small circle at the bottom end of each line. Try drawing them freehand.
1. Look at each picture and spot the circles in it.
2. Sketch the circles in the right places and sizes.
3. Compare your freehand circles with the pictures and see how round they are.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing uses round circles of the sizes and positions described. Freehand circles are usually uneven, which is why a compass is introduced next.

Mark a point 'P' in your notebook. Then, mark as many points as possible, in different directions, that are 4 cm away from P.
Think: Imagine marking all the points of 4 cm distance from the point P. How would they look?
Try to draw it and verify if it is correct by taking some points on the curve and checking if their distances from P are indeed 4 cm.
Explore, if you have not already done so, and see if a compass can be used for this purpose.

1. Predict first: mark P and then every point that is exactly 4 cm from P. What shape will the dots make?
2. Put the 0 cm mark of the ruler on P, never the end of the ruler, and mark a point at 4 cm. Turn the ruler and mark another.
3. After many turns the dots make a round shape around P: a circle with centre P.

content.text:
Worked example: Mark a point P in your notebook. Then mark as many points as possible, in different directions, that are 4 cm away from P.
1. Mark P in the middle of the page.
2. Place the ruler with 0 cm at P and mark a point at 4 cm.
3. Turn the ruler to another direction and mark another point at 4 cm from P; repeat in many directions.
4. Notice the points form a round shape around P.
Answer: All the points you mark lie on a round curve around P, each exactly 4 cm from P. With enough points they join into a circle of radius 4 cm.

concepts.concept_name: All the points 4 cm from P

content.text:
You can start by marking a few points of distance 4 cm from P using the compass. How can this be done?
You will have to open up the compass against a ruler (see Fig. 8.2) such that the distance between the tip of the compass and the pencil is 4 cm.
Now, try to get the full curve.
Hint: Keep the point of the compass fixed moving only the pencil.
What is the shape of the curve? It is a circle!
Take a point on the circle. What will be its distance from P, equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? Similarly, what will be the distance between P and another point on the circle?
As shown in the figure, the point P is called the centre of the circle and the distance between the centre and any point on the circle is called the radius of the circle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: with the tip fixed on P and the pencil swung around, is any point of the curve nearer to P than 4 cm?
2. Open the compass against a ruler until the tip and the pencil are 4 cm apart. Fix the tip at P and move only the pencil.
3. The pencil stays 4 cm from the tip all the way round. The fixed point is the centre and that fixed distance is the radius.
4. Keeko thinks the compass opening is the width of the whole circle. It is only the radius; the width is twice as much.

content.text:
Worked example: How can a compass be used to mark points that are 4 cm from P?
1. Place the compass next to a ruler and open it until the tip and the pencil point are 4 cm apart.
2. Put the tip firmly on P.
3. Keep the tip fixed and move only the pencil all the way round.
Answer: Open the compass so that the distance between its tip and the pencil is 4 cm (check against a ruler). Fix the tip at P and swing the pencil; every point it marks is 4 cm from P, giving a full circle.

concepts.concept_name: The compass draws the circle: centre and radius

content.text:
Worked example: Take a point on the circle drawn with centre P and radius 4 cm. Is its distance from P equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? What about any other point on the circle?
1. The pencil stayed exactly 4 cm from the tip all the time.
2. So every point on the circle is 4 cm from P.
3. This fixed distance is the radius; P is the centre.
Answer: Equal to 4 cm for every point on the circle. P is called the centre and the distance from the centre to any point on the circle is called the radius.

A circle is all the points at one fixed distance from the centre.
Set the compass opening against a ruler before drawing, and keep the tip fixed.
Touching circles have centres two radii apart; concentric circles share a centre.

topic_objective.objective_text: Students recognise circles in artwork, explain that a circle is all the points at one fixed distance from its centre, and draw a circle of a given radius with a compass set against a ruler.

topics.detailed_summary: A circle is every point at the same distance, the radius, from one point, the centre; the compass keeps that distance fixed while the pencil moves.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students describe how the circles in each artwork picture touch, overlap or share a centre, and say why freehand circles come out uneven.
Students mark points that are 4 cm from a point P with a ruler in many directions and say that together they form a circle with centre P.
Students open a compass to 4 cm against a ruler, draw the circle with the tip fixed at the centre, and state that every point on it is one radius from the centre.
Students set a radius on the compass tool, fix the centre, draw circles that touch, overlap or share a centre, and check points on them with a ruler.

concepts.concept_name: Waves from Half Circles: Q1

content.text:
$1$. Draw $AB = 8\text{ cm}$ with a ruler.
$2$. Mark $X$ on $AB$ at $4\text{ cm}$ from $A$.
$3$. Set the compass to $2\text{ cm}$; put the tip at the point $2\text{ cm}$ from $A$ and draw a half circle above $AB$ from $A$ to $X$.
$4$. Put the tip at the point $6\text{ cm}$ from $A$ (which is $2\text{ cm}$ from $B$) and draw a half circle below $AB$ from $X$ to $B$.
$5$. Shade both half circles with vertical lines.
Answer: $AB = 8\text{ cm}$, $AX = XB = 4\text{ cm}$. Each half circle has diameter $4\text{ cm}$, so radius $2\text{ cm}$. First half circle: tip at the point $2\text{ cm}$ from $A$ on $AB$, drawn above the line. Second half circle: tip at the point $6\text{ cm}$ from $A$ on $AB$, drawn below the line.

content.text:
$1$. Draw a line $AB$ of any length $L$.
$2$. Mark the middle point $X$.
$3$. Set the compass to $L \div 4$ and draw the first half circle above $AB$ from $A$ to $X$.
$4$. Draw the second half circle below $AB$ from $X$ to $B$ with the same radius.
Answer: Open ended. For a central line of length $L$, each half circle has diameter $L \div 2$ and radius $L \div 4$. Example: $L = 10\text{ cm}$ gives two half circles of diameter $5\text{ cm}$ and radius $2.5\text{ cm}$; $L = 12\text{ cm}$ gives radius $3\text{ cm}$.

Set the compass to $L \div 4$ and draw the first half circle above $AB$ from $A$ to $X$.
Draw the second half circle below $AB$ from $X$ to $B$ with the same radius.
content.answer_tex: Open ended. For a central line of length $L$, each half circle has diameter $L \div 2$ and radius $L \div 4$. Example: $L = 10\text{ cm}$ gives two half circles of diameter $5\text{ cm}$ and radius $2.5\text{ cm}$; $L = 12\text{ cm}$ gives radius $3\text{ cm}$.

source: Draw a person made of a circle for the head, a short straight neck line below it, and a body that is a rectangle whose top edge is a curved arc dipping in the middle. How will you draw the curved top of the body with a compass? Where should the tip be placed and what radius should be used?
never_show: the finished person before the answer
video_script.wrong_move: Kiko puts the tip inside the body, on the figure itself. The arc then bulges upward like a hill, but the body top must dip in the middle, so the bubble is struck.
maths_rules: Head: a full circle drawn with the compass. Neck: a short straight line below the head.
Body: two vertical sides and a flat bottom; the two top corners are 6 cm apart, so each is 6 / 2 = 3 cm from the middle line.
The top edge is an arc of a circle joining the two top corners and dipping in the middle.
Tip on the middle line, 4 cm above the line joining the top corners; each top corner is then 5 cm from the tip (3-4-5 right triangle, checked with a ruler).
The lowest spot of the arc is 5 cm below the tip, which is 5 - 4 = 1 cm below the top corners.
Slip: a tip inside the body gives an arc that bulges upward, not one that dips.
video_script.payoff_line: The tip goes above the body, and the opening reaches both top corners.

final_answer.value: open ended; the head is a circle; the body top is an arc with the tip above the body on the line through its middle, and the opening is the distance from the tip to a top corner (for a body 6 cm wide: tip 4 cm above the top corners, opening 5 cm)
final_answer.spoken: the head is a circle, and the body top is an arc drawn with the tip above the body, in line with its middle, and an opening that reaches both top corners; for a body six centimetres wide the opening is five centimetres

video_script.substitution: A body six centimetres wide, with the tip four centimetres above the line joining the top corners.
video_script.wrong_answer: put the tip inside the body

media.teaching_notes: One idea: an arc that dips in the middle is drawn with the tip above the figure, not on it. Watch for the slip of placing the tip inside the body, which gives an arc that bulges upward.

interaction_points.answer: open ended; the head is a circle; the body top is an arc with the tip above the body on the line through its middle, and the opening is the distance from the tip to a top corner (for a body 6 cm wide: tip 4 cm above the top corners, opening 5 cm)

source: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.
never_show: the finished eye before the answer
video_script.wrong_move: Kiko wants to put the tip above the eye for the upper arc. A tip above makes the arc bulge downward like a bowl, but the upper arc must bulge upward, so the bubble is struck.
maths_rules: Each curve of the eye is an arc, a part of a circle.
The corners are on the middle line, 6 cm apart, so each is 6 / 2 = 3 cm from the centre of the eye.
Upper arc: tip 4 cm below the middle line, opening 5 cm; each corner is 5 cm from the tip (3-4-5 right triangle, checked with a ruler); the arc rises 5 - 4 = 1 cm above the middle line.
Lower arc: tip 4 cm above the middle line, the same opening 5 cm; the arc falls 1 cm below the middle line.
Same opening and equal distance from the middle give two identical arcs, so the eye is symmetrical and 1 + 1 = 2 cm tall.
Slip: a tip above the eye makes the arc bulge downward, not upward.
video_script.payoff_line: Both arcs use one opening, and the two tips sit equally far from the middle.

final_answer.value: open ended; both arcs have equal radius, the tips lie on the line through the middle of the eye, one on each side, equally far from the middle (for an eye 6 cm wide: tips 4 cm from the middle line, opening 5 cm)
final_answer.spoken: both arcs use one opening, and the two tips sit equally far from the middle; for an eye six centimetres wide the opening is five centimetres and each tip is four centimetres from the middle line

video_script.substitution: An eye six centimetres wide, with tips four centimetres from the middle line and an opening of five centimetres.
video_script.wrong_answer: put the tip above the eye

topics.summary: An arc is a part of a circle; to draw it between two points, place the tip off the figure and swing a radius that reaches both points.

content.text: 1. A Person: How will you draw this? This figure has two components. You might have figured out a way of drawing the first part. For drawing the second part, see this. The challenge here is to find out where to place the tip of the compass and the radius to be taken for drawing this curve. concepts.concept_name: Arcs for A Person and Eyes: Q1

content.text:
$1$. Draw the head circle with the compass.
$2$. Draw the neck as a short vertical line below the circle.
$3$. Draw the body as a rectangle without the top edge: two vertical sides and a flat bottom.
$4$. Fix a radius and try the tip at different spots above the body until the arc from one top corner to the other touches the bottom of the neck line.
$5$. Draw the arc and rub out the trial marks.
Answer: Open ended. The head is a circle. The body is a rectangle with vertical sides and a flat bottom, and its top is an arc of a circle joining the two top corners and dipping down in the middle. The compass tip goes above the body (outside it, on the line through the middle of the body) at a point found by trial, and the radius is the distance from that tip to the top corners. The neck line joins the bottom of the head to the lowest point of the arc.

concepts.concept_name: Arcs for A Person and Eyes: Q2

content.text:
$1$. Draw two light horizontal guide lines (supporting lines) that help to place the compass tips.
$2$. Choose a radius and place the tip at $B$ to draw the upper curve between the two corners.
$3$. Place the tip at $A$, the same distance from the middle on the other side, and with the same radius draw the lower curve.
$4$. Fill the pupil circle in the middle.
$5$. Repeat for the second eye and adjust until both eyes are symmetrical and identical.
Answer: Open ended. The upper and lower curves are arcs of equal radius. Their compass tips (points $A$ and $B$) lie on the line through the middle of the eye, one on each side, equally far from the middle, so that the eye is symmetrical. Draw a filled circle in the middle as the pupil.

maths_rules: AB = 12 cm; X is halfway, so AX = XB = 12 / 2 = 6 cm.
Half of 6 cm is 6 / 2 = 3 cm; the opening must be bigger than 3 cm, so take 5 cm.

First wave: tip 4 cm below the line, straight below the middle of AX (3 cm from A); each end of the wave is 5 cm from the tip (3-4-5 right triangle, checked with a ruler); the arc above the line is 5 - 4 = 1 cm high.
Second wave: tip 4 cm above the line, straight above the middle of XB (9 cm from A), the same opening 5 cm; the arc below the line is 1 cm deep.
Check: same opening 5 cm and same tip distance 4 cm, so both waves are 1 cm high and identical.

content.text:
$1$. Draw the central line and mark the chord for each wave.
$2$. Choose one radius bigger than half the chord.
$3$. For the upper arc, place the tip below the line on the perpendicular through the middle of the chord, at a fixed distance, and draw the arc above the line.
$4$. For the lower arc, place the tip above the line at the same distance from the line and use the same radius.
$5$. Check that both arcs look identical.
Answer: Open ended. Both waves are arcs of the same radius on the same length of chord. A correct drawing shows two identical arcs, one above the line and one below the line, each shorter than a half circle.

maths_rules: Rectangle ABCD: A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left; the sides are AB, BC, CD, DA.
Valid names go round in order: ABCD, BCDA, CDAB, DABC one way and ADCB, DCBA, CBAD, BADC the other way.
Rule: every two letters side by side in a name are the two ends of one side.
ABDC is not valid: B and D are opposite corners, so BD is a diagonal. ACBD is not valid: A and C are opposite corners, so AC is a diagonal.
Check: BCDA uses BC, CD, DA, which are all sides.

topics.summary: A rectangle has opposite sides equal and all angles 90°; a square has all sides equal and all angles 90°, so every square is also a rectangle.

content.text:
Now, let us look at some basic figures having straight lines in their boundary.
What shapes are these? Yes, these are our familiar squares and rectangles. But what makes them squares and rectangles?
Consider this rectangle ABCD.
The points A, B, C and D are the corners of the rectangle. Lines AB, BC, CD and DA are its sides. Its angles are ∠A, ∠B, ∠C and ∠D.
The blue sides AB and CD are called opposite sides, as they lie opposite to each other. Likewise, AD and BC is the other pair of opposite sides.
Recall that, in a rectangle:
R1) The opposite sides are equal in length, and
R2) All the angles are 90°.
As in the case of rectangles, the corners and sides are defined for a square in the same manner.
A square satisfies the following two properties:
S1) All the sides are equal, and
S2) All the angles are 90°.

1. Predict first: a door, a notebook, a chessboard square. What do they share, and what is different?
2. A rectangle satisfies R1, the opposite sides are equal in length, and R2, all the angles are 90°.

4. A square also has opposite sides equal, so it meets R1 and R2 too. Keeko thinks a square is not a rectangle, but it is a special rectangle.
5. Four equal sides are not enough. A slanted diamond has four equal sides and is not a square.

content.text:
See the rectangle in Fig. 8.4 and the name given to it: ABCD. This rectangle can also be named in other ways, BCDA, CDAB, DABC, ADCB, DCBA, CBAD and BADC. So, can a rectangle be named using any combination of the labels around its corners? No! For example, it cannot be named ABDC or ACBD. Can you see what names are allowed and what names are not?
In a valid name, the corners occur in an order of travel around the rectangle, starting from any corner.

1. Predict first: a rectangle ABCD can be called BCDA. Can it also be called ABDC?
2. In a valid name the corners come in an order of travel round the figure, starting from any corner and going either way.
3. ABDC goes from B to D, and BD is a diagonal, not a side. So ABDC is not a name for the rectangle.
4. Check each pair of neighbouring letters: it must be a side.

content.text:
Worked example: A rectangle ABCD has corners A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). Besides ABCD it can be named BCDA, CDAB, DABC, ADCB, DCBA, CBAD and BADC. Can a rectangle be named using any combination of the labels around its corners? What names are allowed and what names are not?
1. Check that each pair of letters next to each other in the name is a side of the rectangle.
2. ABDC fails because B to D is a diagonal, not a side.
3. So go round the rectangle one corner after another.
Answer: No. ABDC and ACBD are not allowed. In a valid name the corners come in order, going round the rectangle, starting from any corner and going in either direction.

maths_rules: A: diamond 8 dots wide and 8 dots tall, so half-spans 4 and 4; every side goes 4 across and 4 down, so the 4 sides are equal, and the corners fit a book corner: a square.

B: diamond 6 dots wide and 8 dots tall, half-spans 3 and 4; every side goes 3 across and 4 down (3 x 3 + 4 x 4 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5 x 5, so each side is 5 dot steps); sides equal but the top corner is sharper than a book corner: not a square.
C: diamond 10 dots wide and 8 dots tall, half-spans 5 and 4; sides equal but the top corner is wider than a book corner: not a square.
D: a small tilted rectangle with two long sides and two short sides: not a square.
Only A has four equal sides and four book corners.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it out: Q1

content.text:
$1$. A square needs $4$ equal sides and $4$ angles of $90^\circ$.
$2$. $A$ has equal width and height, so its sides and angles are equal: a square.
$3$. $B$ and $C$ have unequal widths and heights, so they are diamonds whose angles are not $90^\circ$.
$4$. $D$ has two long and two short sides, so it is a rectangle, not a square.
Answer: $A$ is a square.

D has two long and two short sides, so it is a rectangle, not a square.

source: A square piece of paper has all its sides equal and all angles 90 degrees. It is rotated. Is it still a square? Are all the sides still equal? Are all the angles still 90 degrees?

video_script.wrong_move: Kiko thinks a square turned on its corner is a different shape, because it looks like a diamond. Rotation changes only how the paper stands. The sides and the angles are the same ones as before, so the bubble is struck.
maths_rules: A square has S1 all four sides equal and S2 all four angles 90 degrees.
Rotation turns a shape round without bending or stretching it, so every length stays the same.
Rotation keeps every angle the same too, so each angle of the rotated paper is still 90 degrees.
The rotated paper has both properties of a square, so it is a square.
By the same reasoning, a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.

source: Is it possible to reason out if the sides are equal or not, and if the angles are right or not, without using any measuring instruments? Can we do this by only looking at the position of corners in the dot grid?

maths_rules: Take P at the top. The corner Q is 3 dots right and 2 dots down from P. The corner R is 2 dots left and 3 dots down from Q. The corner S is 3 dots left and 2 dots up from R. Then P is 2 dots right and 3 dots up from S.
Every side uses the counts 3 and 2, so every side has the same length (the square of that length is 3 x 3 + 2 x 2 = 9 + 4 = 13 square dot steps, but the video only compares the counts).
P to Q is 3 across and 2 down; turning this step by a quarter turn (90 degrees) swaps the counts: Q to R is 2 across and 3 down.
At every corner the next step is the previous step turned a quarter turn, so every angle is 90 degrees.
A rotation keeps lengths, so each turned step is as long as the one before it.

topics.summary: Rotating a figure changes neither its lengths nor its angles, so a tilted square is still a square.

content.text:
Here is a square piece of paper having all its sides equal in length and all angles equal to 90°. It is rotated as shown in the figure. Is it still a square?
Let us check if the rotated paper still satisfies the properties of a square.
Are all the sides still equal? Yes.
Are all the angles still 90°? Yes.
Rotating a square does not change its lengths and angles.
Therefore, this rotated figure satisfies both the properties of a square and so, it is a square.
By the same reasoning, a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.

1. Predict first: turn a square piece of paper so its corners point up, down, left and right. Is it still a square?
2. Check S1: the sides are still equal, because turning does not stretch anything.
3. Check S2: the angles are still 90°, because turning does not bend anything.
4. So the tilted figure is a square. A rotated rectangle is a rectangle in the same way.

content.text:
Worked example: A square piece of paper has all its sides equal and all angles 90°. It is rotated (tilted so it looks like a diamond). Is it still a square? Are all the sides still equal? Are all the angles still 90°?
1. Rotating does not change lengths.
2. Rotating does not change angles.
3. So both square properties S1 and S2 still hold.
Answer: Yes, it is still a square. All the sides are still equal and all the angles are still 90°, because rotating a square does not change its lengths and angles. In the same way a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a tilted figure has its corners on dots. Can you tell that its sides are equal without a ruler?
2. Go from one corner to the next by a number of dots across and a number down. If every side uses the same two numbers, the sides are equal.
3. At the next corner swap the two numbers: across becomes down. That is a turn of 90°.
4. So the dot positions alone show equal sides and right angles.

maths_rules: Square 1: centre O, corners 4 dots up, 4 right, 4 down and 4 left of O. Each side goes 4 across and 4 down or up, so the 4 sides are equal; the sides turn through a quarter turn, so each angle is 90 degrees.

Square 2: P at (0, 0), Q at (3, 1), R at (2, 4), S at (-1, 3). The steps are 3 right 1 up, 1 left 3 up, 3 left 1 down, 1 right 3 down. Every side uses the counts 3 and 1, and each step is the previous one turned a quarter turn, so it is a square.

Rectangle: P at (0, 0), Q at (2, 2), R at (-1, 5), S at (-3, 3). The steps are 2 right 2 up, 3 left 3 up, 2 left 2 down, 3 right 3 down. Opposite sides use the same counts, so they are equal; the two kinds of step point along the two diagonals of the grid squares, at 90 degrees; the sides are not all equal, so it is a rectangle and not a square.
Check with a ruler for the sides and the corner of a book for the angles.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it out: Q1

content.text:
$1$. Draw the rectangle on dots, counting dots along each side.
$2$. From each corner of the rectangle, move one dot diagonally outwards (same count each time).
$3$. Draw an equal square at each of the four places, counting the same number of dots for every square.
$4$. Use the same counts on the left and right, top and bottom so the figure is symmetrical.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing shows a rectangle with four equal squares around it placed in the same way at each corner. Book hint: draw the rectangle and then leave one dot distance diagonally to place the four smaller squares.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it out: Q2

content.text:
$1$. Pick dots as corners so that each side goes the same number of dots across and down for a square.
$2$. Join the corners with a ruler.
$3$. Measure the sides with the ruler.
$4$. Check the angles with a protractor or a set square.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: each rotated square has $4$ equal sides and $4$ angles of $90^\circ$; each rotated rectangle has equal opposite sides and $4$ angles of $90^\circ$. For example a diamond with corners $4$ dots up, $4$ dots right, $4$ dots down and $4$ dots left of its centre is a square.

concepts.concept_name: Rotated Squares and Rectangles: Q1

content.text:
$1$. Count how many dots across and how many down it takes to go from one corner to the next.
$2$. If every side uses the same counts, the sides are equal.
$3$. If the next side uses the counts swapped for a turn (across and down exchanged), the angle is $90^\circ$.
Answer: Yes. The positions of the dots make it possible. Moving from one corner to the next by the same number of dots across and down, and turning with the counts swapped, gives equal sides and right angles.

media.description: Construction Stepper. Pick the right instrument. Build a square step by step. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: A square or a rectangle is built in order: one side, perpendiculars at both ends, the other corners at the right length, then the last side; the properties fix the lengths and angles that are not measured.
tool_config.title: Construction Stepper
tool_config.screen: A drawing sheet with a ruler, a protractor and a compass; a list of steps that unlock one at a time; a measuring read-out for every side and angle; a Check button.
feedback: Measuring from the end of the ruler instead of the zero mark gives a side that is too short, and the Check button shows the actual length.
Marking an equal length on only one perpendicular leaves the figure open, and the tool shows the gap.
A solved card shows every step in order with the final sides and angles.
challenges: A square of side 5 cm: how long is the fourth side? (5 cm)
A rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm: how long is the side opposite the 6 cm side? (6 cm)
A square of side 3 cm: what is each angle? (90°)
A rectangle 8 cm by 3 cm: how many lengths must you mark by compass or ruler? (two, one on each perpendicular)
A rectangle 5 cm by 2 cm: how long is the side opposite the 2 cm side? (2 cm)
A rectangle 7 cm by 4 cm: what is each angle? (90°)

hint_ladder.text: Which side is drawn first?

Mark the length from the card on each perpendicular, then join the two marks.

maths_rules: A square has all 4 sides equal and all 4 angles 90 degrees.
Draw PQ = 6 cm with the zero mark of the ruler at P.
At P, place the protractor with its centre at P and its baseline along PQ, mark 90 degrees and draw the perpendicular through P; mark S on it with PS = 6 cm.
At Q draw the perpendicular to PQ and mark R on it with QR = 6 cm; a compass with its opening kept at 6 cm can be used instead.
Join R and S; check RS = 6 cm and the angles at R and S are 90 degrees.
The finished square has PQ = QR = RS = SP = 6 cm.

Worked example: How would you construct a square with a side of 6 cm? A square PQRS of side length 6 cm is constructed.

4. At Q draw the perpendicular to PQ and mark R with QR = 6 cm (with the compass: keep the radius at 6 cm and put the tip at Q).
5. Join R and S. Check RS = 6 cm, ∠R = 90°, ∠S = 90°.

concepts.concept_name: Constructing a Rectangle: Q1

content.text:
$1$. Draw $AB = 4\text{ cm}$.
$2$. Draw perpendiculars at $A$ and $B$.
$3$. Mark $D$ on the one at $A$ so that $AD = 6\text{ cm}$, and $C$ on the one at $B$ so that $BC = 6\text{ cm}$.
$4$. Join $D$ and $C$.
$5$. Measure: opposite sides are equal ($4$ and $4$, $6$ and $6$) and all angles are $90^\circ$.
Answer: Rectangle $ABCD$ with $AB = CD = 4\text{ cm}$, $AD = BC = 6\text{ cm}$ and $\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = \angle D = 90^\circ$. Both properties hold.

$1$. Draw one side and the two perpendiculars at its ends.
$2$. The two perpendiculars stay the same distance apart, so the opposite side is the same length as the first side.
$3$. So opposite sides are always equal.

topics.summary: Between two opposite sides of a rectangle the shortest XY equals the side length, when X and Y are level; the longest XY is a diagonal.

content.text:
Construct a rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.
Imagine X to be a point that can be moved anywhere along the side AD. Similarly, imagine Y to be a point that can be moved anywhere along the side BC. Note that X can also be placed on the end point A or D. Similarly, Y can also be placed on the end point B or C.
At which positions will the points X and Y be at their closest? When do you think they will be the farthest? What does your intuition say? Discuss with your classmates. (Math Talk)
Now, verify your guesses by placing the points X and Y on the sides and measure how near or far they are.
The distance between X and Y can be obtained by measuring the length of the line XY.
How does the minimum distance between the points X and Y compare to the length of AB?

concepts.concept_name: Setting up the rectangle and guessing

content.text:
Worked example: In rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, X moves along side AD and Y moves along side BC. At which positions will the points X and Y be at their closest? When do you think they will be the farthest? What does your intuition say? Discuss with your classmates.
1. Try several positions with a ruler.
2. XY is 7 cm whenever X and Y are at equal distances from A and B.
3. XY is longest when X and Y are at opposite corners.
Answer: Closest: when X and Y are the same distance from A and B respectively (for example X = A and Y = B), where XY = 7 cm. Farthest: when X is at one corner and Y at the opposite corner (X = A and Y = C, or X = D and Y = B), where XY is a diagonal of about 8 cm 1 mm (√65 cm).

Worked example: How does the minimum distance between the points X and Y compare to the length of AB (7 cm)?
1. Measure XY when X and Y are level (same distance from A and B).
2. You get 7 cm each time, which is the length of AB.
Answer: The minimum distance of XY is 7 cm, which is equal to AB.

content.text:
Change the positions of X and Y to check if there are other positions where they are at their nearest or farthest. You could construct multiple copies of the rectangle and try out various positions of X and Y.
How will you keep track of the lengths XY for different positions of X and Y?
Here is one way of doing it. Suppose here are some of the positions of X and Y that you have considered:
When X is 5 mm away from A and Y is 3 cm away from B, XY = ___ cm ___ mm.
When X is 1 cm away from A and Y is 1 cm away from B, XY = ___ cm ___ mm.
When X is 2 cm away from A and Y is 4 cm away from B, XY = ___ cm ___ mm and so on.
Is there a shorthand way of writing it down? In all the sentences, only the position of X, Y and the length XY changes. So we could write this as: (table: Distance of X from A, Distance of Y from B, Length of XY)

content.text:
1. Predict first: if X and Y are the same distance from A and B, what shape is ABYX?
2. X and Y are at the same height, so XY runs straight across. All four angles of ABYX are 90° and opposite sides are equal, so ABYX is a rectangle and XY equals AB.
3. The farthest apart are opposite corners: X at A and Y at C, or X at D and Y at B.
4. Then XY is a diagonal, AC or BD, about 8.1 cm for this rectangle.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students construct a rectangle with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, place X on AD and Y on BC, and predict where X and Y are closest and where they are farthest.
Students measure XY for chosen positions of X and Y and record each case as a row of a table with the distance of X from A, the distance of Y from B and the length XY.
Students show that equal distances of X from A and of Y from B give XY equal to AB and ABYX a rectangle, and that the farthest XY is a diagonal of the rectangle.

concepts.concept_name: How Far Apart Can Two Points Be?: Q1

content.text:
$1$. Across the rectangle the distance is $7\text{ cm}$; the up and down difference between the two points changes.
$2$. $(a)$: the difference is $3\text{ cm} - 5\text{ mm} = 2.5\text{ cm}$, $XY = \sqrt{49 + 6.25} \approx 7.4\text{ cm}$.
$3$. $(b)$: the difference is $0$, $XY = 7\text{ cm}$.
$4$. $(c)$: the difference is $4\text{ cm} - 2\text{ cm} = 2\text{ cm}$, $XY = \sqrt{49 + 4} \approx 7.3\text{ cm}$.
Answer: $(a)$: $7\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ mm}$, $(b)$: $7\text{ cm}$ and $0\text{ mm}$, $(c)$: $7\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ mm}$
steps: Across the rectangle the distance is 7 cm; the up and down difference between the two points changes.
a) the difference is 3 cm − 5 mm = 2.5 cm, XY = √(49 + 6.25) ≈ 7.4 cm.
b) the difference is 0, XY = 7 cm.
c) the difference is 4 cm − 2 cm = 2 cm, XY = √(49 + 4) ≈ 7.3 cm.
content.answer: a) 7 cm and 4 mm, b) 7 cm and 0 mm, c) 7 cm and 3 mm

$2$. So $XY$ is parallel to $AB$ and as long as $AB$: $7\text{ cm}$.

content.text:
Explore: What about constructing a rectangle that can be divided into two identical squares? Can you try it?
It is wise to first plan and then construct. But how do we plan? Can you think of a way?
One way is to visualise the final figure by drawing a rough diagram of it.
What can we infer from this figure? Can you identify the equal sides? Since the two squares are identical, AB = BC and FE = ED. Since ABEF and BCDE are squares, all the sides in each of the squares are equal. This is written as: AF = AB = BE = FE; BE = BC = CD = ED. So, all the shorter lines are equal!
A convention is followed to represent equal sides. It is done by putting a '|' on the line. Refer to the rough figure.
Using this analysis, can you try constructing it? Remember, all that was asked for is a rectangle that can be divided into two identical squares and with no measurements imposed.
To draw the rectangle ACDF, one could assign any length to AF. For example, if we assign AF = 4 cm, then what must the length of AC be?
Explore: Can the rectangle now be completed?

content.text:
1. Predict first: can a rectangle 4 cm by 2.5 cm be cut into two identical squares?
2. Two identical squares need the length to be 2 times the breadth. Here 2 times 2.5 cm is 5 cm, not 4 cm.
3. Three identical squares need the length to be 3 times the breadth. A rectangle 7 cm by 2 cm fails, because 3 times 2 cm is 6 cm.
4. Many answers are possible, so test any pair with the length-to-breadth rule.

content.text:
$1$. Draw a rough diagram: $AB = BC$ and $FE = ED$, and all the short lines are equal $(AF = AB = BE = FE = BC = CD = ED)$.
$2$. Draw $AF = 4\text{ cm}$.
$3$. Draw a line perpendicular to $AF$ at $A$. With the compass tip at $A$ and radius $AF$, mark $B$ on this line.
$4$. Keep the same radius and mark $C$ beyond $B$ so that $BC = AF$.
$5$. Do the same at $F$ to place the other corners and complete the rectangle $ACDF$.
Answer: $AC = 8\text{ cm}$. The rectangle is $8\text{ cm}$ by $4\text{ cm}$.

content.text:
$1$. Draw the $8\text{ cm}$ by $4\text{ cm}$ rectangle.
$2$. The square must fit between top and bottom, so its side is $4\text{ cm}$.
$3$. Leave $(8\text{ cm} - 4\text{ cm}) \div 2 = 2\text{ cm}$ on each side.
$4$. Mark points $2\text{ cm}$ in from each short side and draw the vertical lines of the square.
Answer: The square has side $4\text{ cm}$. Its left and right sides are $2\text{ cm}$ away from the left and right sides of the rectangle.

media.title: Diagonal Explorer
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 8 'Playing with Constructions' (Diagonals of Rectangles). Draw both diagonals. Compare. Find a pattern. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Diagonal Explorer. Draw both diagonals. Compare. Find a pattern. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

content.text:
In rectangle PQRS, the right angles at P and R are referred to as opposite angles. The other pair of opposite angles are the right angles at Q and S.
Observe that a diagonal divides each of the pair of opposite angles into two smaller angles. In the figure, the diagonal PR divides angle R into two smaller angles which we simply call g and h. The diagonal also divides angle P into c and d. Are g and h equal? Are c and d equal?
First predict the answers, and then measure the angles. What do you observe? Identify pairs of angles that are equal.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the diagonal PR cuts the 90° corner at P into two angles. Will the two angles be equal?
2. Measure them in the 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle: about 34° and about 56°. They are not equal, but they add up to 90°.
3. With both diagonals drawn there are eight small angles. The four next to the sides PQ and SR match, and the four next to PS and QR match.
4. So angles come in two sizes, and each pair of sizes adds up to 90°.

content.text:
Worked example: In rectangle PQRS the diagonal PR divides angle R into g and h, and divides angle P into c and d. Predict, then measure: are g and h equal? Are c and d equal? a) Are g and h equal? b) Are c and d equal?
1. Draw a rectangle that is not a square, for example 6 cm by 4 cm, and its diagonal PR.
2. Measure c, d at P and g, h at R with a protractor.
3. For 6 cm by 4 cm the angles are about 34° and 56°, so c and d differ.
4. In a square both angles are 45°.
5. In each case the two small angles add up to 90°.
Answer: a) g and h are not equal unless the rectangle is a square; b) c and d are not equal unless the rectangle is a square. In every rectangle g + h = 90° and c + d = 90°.

content.text:
Worked example: In rectangle PQRS, with both diagonals drawn, the eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h (at P: c and d; at Q: e and f; at R: g and h; at S: a and b; c is next to side PS, d next to PQ, e next to QP, f next to QR, g next to RQ, h next to RS, a next to SR, b next to SP). Measure them. Which angles are equal?
1. Draw a rectangle that is not a square and both its diagonals.
2. Measure all eight angles with a protractor.
3. The four angles next to the long sides come out equal: d, e, a, h.
4. The four angles next to the short sides come out equal: c, f, g, b.
5. Each pair from the two groups adds up to 90°.
Answer: d = e = a = h (the four angles next to the sides PQ and SR) and c = f = g = b (the four angles next to the sides PS and QR). Also c + d = 90°.

concepts.concept_name: When a Diagonal Splits a Corner Equally: Q1

content.text:
$1$. Try rectangles whose sides are different: the diagonal splits the right angle into unequal parts.
$2$. Make the adjacent sides equal, for example $5\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$.
$3$. Draw the diagonal and measure: both parts are $45^\circ$.
$4$. So only a square works.
Answer: The two adjacent sides must be equal, that is, the rectangle must be a square. Then each diagonal divides the opposite angles into $45^\circ$ and $45^\circ$.

concepts.concept_name: When a Diagonal Splits a Corner Equally: Q2

content.text:
$1$. Look at your table of sides and the eight angles for several rectangles.
$2$. Notice which numbers repeat in each row.
$3$. Write each repeated pattern as a rule.
$4$. Check the special case of a square separately.
Answer: In every rectangle: opposite sides are equal and all angles are $90^\circ$; the two diagonals are equal in length (and cut each other into equal halves); each diagonal divides the opposite angles into two angles that add up to $90^\circ$; the angles the diagonals make with the sides are equal in pairs $(d = e = a = h$ and $c = f = g = b)$. If the adjacent sides are equal (a square), each diagonal divides the opposite angles into $45^\circ$ and $45^\circ$; if not, the two parts are unequal.

concepts.concept_name: When a Diagonal Splits a Corner Equally: Q3

content.text:
$1$. Try many different rectangles and see if the law holds each time.
$2$. Notice that measurements are only close, not exact.
$3$. Look for a reason using properties already known, for example that opposite sides are parallel.
$4$. A reason that works for every rectangle makes us sure.
Answer: Measuring a few examples cannot prove a law for every rectangle, because measurements are approximate and we cannot try all rectangles. We need a reason that works for any rectangle, such as using what we know (opposite sides equal, all angles $90^\circ$, alternate angles at parallel sides) to explain why the pattern must hold.

content.text:
$1$. Draw $AB$ of any length. At $B$ draw a perpendicular line $(90^\circ)$.
$2$. At $A$, use the protractor to draw a $60^\circ$ angle with $AB$. Where this ray meets the perpendicular from $B$, mark $C$.
$3$. Through $A$, draw a line perpendicular to $AB$. This is the line on which $D$ lies, and angle $A$ is now $60^\circ + 30^\circ$.
$4$. Find $D$. Method $1$: draw a perpendicular to $BC$ at $C$, and $D$ is where it meets the line through $A$. Method $2$: with the compass take length $BC$ and mark $D$ on the line through $A$ so that $AD = BC$.
$5$. Join $CD$. $ABCD$ is the rectangle. Check: $AB = CD$, $AD = BC$ and every angle is $90^\circ$.
Answer: Rectangle $ABCD$ in which the diagonal $AC$ makes $60^\circ$ with side $AB$ and $30^\circ$ with side $AD$ (angle $A = 90^\circ = 60^\circ + 30^\circ$). The side lengths can be chosen freely, as only the angles are given.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it out: Q1

content.text:
$1$. Draw $AB$ of any length. At $B$ draw a perpendicular $(90^\circ)$.
$2$. At $A$, draw a $50^\circ$ angle with $AB$. The ray meets the perpendicular from $B$ at $C$.
$3$. Draw the perpendicular to $AB$ at $A$. Then the other angle at $A$ is $90^\circ - 50^\circ = 40^\circ$.
$4$. Draw a perpendicular to $BC$ at $C$. It meets the line through $A$ at $D$.
$5$. Check: $AB = CD$, $AD = BC$, all angles $90^\circ$.
Answer: Rectangle $ABCD$ in which the diagonal $AC$ makes $50^\circ$ with side $AB$ and $40^\circ$ with side $AD$ (while at $C$ the diagonal makes $50^\circ$ with $CD$ and $40^\circ$ with $CB$). Side lengths are free.
steps: Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular (90°).
At A, draw a 50° angle with AB. The ray meets the perpendicular from B at C.
Draw the perpendicular to AB at A. Then the other angle at A is 90° − 50° = 40°.
Draw a perpendicular to BC at C. It meets the line through A at D.
Check: AB = CD, AD = BC, all angles 90°.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it out: Q2

content.text:
$1$. Draw $AB$ of any length. At $B$ draw a perpendicular.
$2$. At $A$, draw a $45^\circ$ angle with $AB$. It meets the perpendicular at $C$.
$3$. Draw the perpendicular to $AB$ at $A$ (the other angle at $A$ is $90^\circ - 45^\circ = 45^\circ$).
$4$. Draw the perpendicular to $BC$ at $C$. It meets the line through $A$ at $D$.
$5$. Measure the sides: $AB = BC = CD = DA$. It is a square.
Answer: $(a)$: the rectangle is built with $45^\circ$ at $A$, next to $AB$, and $45^\circ$ next to $AD$; $(b)$: all the sides are equal, so it is a square.

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What is the real-life use case?
A carpenter uses a compass to mark exact lengths on a wooden board.

content.text:
$1$. Draw base $DC = 5\text{ cm}$.
$2$. At $C$ draw a line $l$ perpendicular to $DC$ (that is, $90^\circ$).
$3$. With the compass opened to $7\text{ cm}$ and centre $D$, draw an arc that cuts line $l$. The cutting point is $B$ (where $DB = 7\text{ cm}$).
$4$. Draw a perpendicular to $DC$ at $D$ and a perpendicular to $BC$ at $B$. They meet at $A$. (Or use the compass to mark $A$ so that $DA = CB$ and $AB = DC$.)
$5$. Check: $AB = 5\text{ cm}$, $BC = AD$, angles $90^\circ$, diagonal $DB = 7\text{ cm}$.
Answer: Rectangle $ABCD$ with $DC = AB = 5\text{ cm}$ and diagonal $DB = 7\text{ cm}$. The other two sides $AD = BC$ come out about $4.9\text{ cm}$ and all four angles are $90^\circ$.

media.title: Equal Distance Explorer
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 8 'Playing with Constructions' (Equal Distances and Summary). Find the roof point that is as far from B as from C. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Equal Distance Explorer. Find the roof point that is as far from B as from C. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: A point at a given distance from each of two points lies where an arc around the first meets an arc around the second; the arcs meet only if the radius is big enough.
tool_config.title: Equal Distance Explorer
tool_config.screen: Two points B and C with a distance slider; a radius dial; arcs drawn around B and C that sweep out; the crossing point marked with its distance from B and from C.
feedback: Drawing only one arc leaves many possible points; the tool shows the second arc cutting it at the point.
A radius that is too small leaves a gap between the arcs, and the tool shows it.
A solved card shows both arcs and the crossing point with its two distances.
challenges: B and C are 5 cm apart, radius 5 cm: distance of the crossing point from B? (5 cm)
B and C are 6 cm apart, radius 5 cm: how high above the middle of BC is the crossing point? (4 cm)
B and C are 8 cm apart, radius 5 cm: how high above the middle? (3 cm)
B and C are 8 cm apart, radius 3 cm: do the arcs cross? (no)
B and C are 10 cm apart, radius 5 cm: where do the arcs meet? (at the middle of BC)
B and C are 5 cm apart, radius 5 cm: how high is the crossing point above BC, to the nearest tenth? (4.3 cm)

hint_ladder.text: What must be true about the distance of the new point from B and from C?
Draw an arc around each point; they cross where the point is that far from both.
Set the radius from the card and find out whether the arcs reach each other.
The tool shows both arcs and the crossing; a similar card follows.

student_does: Predict whether the arcs will cross before setting the radius.
Set the distance between B and C and the radius.
Read the crossing point and its distance, or say that there is none.

content.text:
STEP 1
Can you complete the figure? Try!
We need to locate the point A that is of distance 5 cm from the points B and C. You might have realised that this can be done using a ruler. However, this leads to a lot of trial and error. This construction can be further simplified. How?
If you have guessed that this can be done by the use of compass, you are right! Go ahead and explore how the point A can be located without trial and error.
There is a similarity between the problem of finding point A in this problem and point B at step 3 of the second solved example of the previous section (see page 209).
STEP 2
Draw a curve that has all its points of 5 cm from the point B; the circle centred at B should be with 5 cm radius.
Does this help in spotting the point A? Construct and explore in the figure.
The point A can be located by finding the correct point on the circle that is of distance 5 cm from the point C. Again, this can be done using a ruler. But can we use a compass for this?
STEP 3
Method 1
Take a radius of 5 cm in the compass and with C as the centre, draw a circle.
Are you able to spot the point A? Check the figure in your notebook. What do you observe?
See the point at which both the circles intersect. How far is it from the point B?
How far is it from C?
Thus, this is the point A!
Think
Was it necessary to draw two full circles to get the point A? We only needed part of both the circles.
Method 2

concepts.concept_name: Example 4: Q

content.text:
$1$. Draw base $DE = 5\text{ cm}$. Draw perpendiculars at $D$ and $E$ and mark $B$ and $C$ each $5\text{ cm}$ up. Draw the door, $1\text{ cm}$ wide and $2\text{ cm}$ tall, on $DE$.
$2$. To find $A$, which is $5\text{ cm}$ from both $B$ and $C$: set the compass to $5\text{ cm}$ and draw an arc from $B$ (the circle of all points $5\text{ cm}$ from $B$).
$3$. With the same $5\text{ cm}$ opening draw an arc from $C$. The two arcs meet at $A$, which is $5\text{ cm}$ from $B$ and $5\text{ cm}$ from $C$. Join $AB$ and $AC$.
$4$. With the compass at $A$ and radius $5\text{ cm}$, draw the arc from $B$ to $C$ (this arc bulges down into the house).
$5$. Check $AB = AC = 5\text{ cm}$.
Answer: A house with $DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 5\text{ cm}$, a door $1\text{ cm}$ wide and $2\text{ cm}$ tall on the base, apex $A$, found as the point $5\text{ cm}$ from both $B$ and $C$, and an arc from $B$ to $C$ drawn with centre $A$ and radius $5\text{ cm}$. Since $BC = 5\text{ cm}$ as well, triangle $ABC$ has all sides $5\text{ cm}$.

Check AB = AC = 5 cm.

content.text:
$1$. Draw $DE = 7\text{ cm}$, then perpendiculars at $D$ and $E$; mark $B$ and $C$ each $7\text{ cm}$ above $D$ and $E$.
$2$. Draw a door on $DE$ (the book's solution uses $2\text{ cm}$ wide and $3\text{ cm}$ tall).
$3$. With the compass at $7\text{ cm}$, draw arcs from $B$ and from $C$. They meet at $A$. Join $AB$ and $AC$.
$4$. With the compass at $A$ and radius $7\text{ cm}$, draw the arc from $B$ to $C$.
$5$. Check: every border line is $7\text{ cm}$.
Answer: A house like the earlier one with all border lines $7\text{ cm}$: $DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 7\text{ cm}$, apex $A$, $7\text{ cm}$ from $B$ and from $C$, and an arc $BC$ with centre $A$ and radius $7\text{ cm}$. The book's solution draws a door $2\text{ cm}$ wide and $3\text{ cm}$ tall.

content.text:
1. Predict first: are there four-sided figures with four equal sides that are not squares?
2. Draw a side BC of 5 cm and a side BA of 5 cm at a slant. The fourth corner D has to be 5 cm from A and from C.
3. Cross two arcs of 5 cm to find D. The figure has four equal sides, but its angles are not 90°.
4. This is a rhombus. Equal sides are not enough for a square, we also need right angles.

content.text:
$1$. Person: draw a circle with the compass for the head, then a neck line and a square for the body.
$2$. Wave: mark equal parts on a central line and draw half circles with the compass, one above and the next below.
$3$. Eyes: draw a light horizontal line. From a point $A$ (above it) draw the lower curve, and from a point $B$ (below it) draw the upper curve, with the same compass opening, so the two arcs meet at the ends.
$4$. Place $A$ and $B$ symmetrically (same distance from the line) so the eye is symmetrical.
$5$. Copy the eye for the second one and add the pupils.
Answer: Open drawing. A correct drawing shows: A Person (a circle for the head, for example radius $2\text{ cm}$, a short neck line, and a $4\text{ cm}$ by $4\text{ cm}$ square body in the book's solution); Wavy Wave (equal half circles drawn alternately above and below a central line); Eyes (two matching lens-shaped eyes, each made from an upper and a lower arc drawn from compass points $A$ (above) and $B$ (below), placed symmetrically, with a filled round pupil).

concepts.concept_name: Figure it out: Q2

content.text:
$1$. Take side length $5\text{ cm}$. Draw $AB = 5\text{ cm}$ and $AC = 5\text{ cm}$ with angle $A$, not equal to $90^\circ$, for example $60^\circ$.
$2$. The fourth point $D$ must be $5\text{ cm}$ from both $B$ and $C$.
$3$. With the compass at $5\text{ cm}$, draw an arc from $B$ and an arc from $C$. They cross at $D$.
$4$. Join $BD$ and $CD$. All four sides $AB$, $AC$, $BD$, $CD$ are $5\text{ cm}$.
$5$. The angles are not $90^\circ$, so it is not a square.
Answer: $(a)$: Yes, a rhombus (diamond) with four equal sides and angles that are not $90^\circ$; $(b)$: yes, it can be constructed with compass arcs.
steps: Take side length 5 cm. Draw AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm with angle A, not equal to 90°, for example 60°.
The fourth point D must be 5 cm from both B and C.
With the compass at 5 cm, draw an arc from B and an arc from C. They cross at D.
Join BD and CD. All four sides AB, AC, BD, CD are 5 cm.
The angles are not 90°, so it is not a square.

topics.summary: Circles and arcs from a compass, rectangles from sides, diagonals or angles, and points equally far from two points.

content.text:
Let's Summarise!
All the points of a circle are at the same distance from its centre. This distance is called the radius of the circle.
A compass can be used to construct circles and their parts.
A rough diagram can be useful in planning how to construct a given figure.
A rectangle can be constructed given the lengths of its sides or that of one of its sides and a diagonal.

content.text:
1. Our opening question is settled: a compass keeps one distance fixed, so every point it draws is equally far from the centre.
2. A rough diagram plans the order of steps, and a rectangle needs its sides, or a side and a diagonal.
3. Still open for you: can you build a rectangle whose diagonal is exactly twice its shorter side?

modules.module_summary: Two arcs of one radius find the point that is the same distance from two points; this builds the house and a figure with four equal sides that is not a square.

objectives.objective_text: Students describe how the circles in each artwork picture touch, overlap or share a centre, and say why freehand circles come out uneven.
Students mark points that are 4 cm from a point P with a ruler in many directions and say that together they form a circle with centre P.
Students open a compass to 4 cm against a ruler, draw the circle with the tip fixed at the centre, and state that every point on it is one radius from the centre.
Students set a radius on the compass tool, fix the centre, draw circles that touch, overlap or share a centre, and check points on them with a ruler.
Students find the radius and the compass tip position for a half circle drawn on a segment, and draw two equal half circles on the two halves of a line, one above and one below.
Students choose a central line length on the wave tool, set the radius for each half circle, and draw waves that alternate above and below the line.
Students draw a circle for a head and an arc for the curved top of a body by trying tip positions above the body until the arc passes through both top corners.
Students draw an almond-shaped eye from an upper and a lower arc of the same radius, with the two compass tips the same distance from the middle line, and fill the pupil.
Students draw two identical arcs, smaller than a half circle, one above and one below a central line, as in the neck of A Person.
Students state R1 and R2 for a rectangle and S1 and S2 for a square, and decide from sides and angles whether a figure is a rectangle, a square or neither.
Students list the valid names of a square or rectangle by travelling round the corners in order, and say why a name that jumps across the figure is not valid.
Students measure sides and angles on the checker tool and classify each figure as a square, a rectangle, a rhombus or none of these.
Students check the two square properties for a turned square and explain that rotation keeps lengths and angles, so the shape does not change.
Students move across and down by dot counts to show that two sides are equal and meet at 90°, without any measuring instrument.
Students draw a rectangle with four equal squares near its corners, and tilted squares and rectangles, on dot paper by counting dots, then check their properties.
Students construct a square PQRS of side 6 cm by drawing PQ, two perpendiculars and two equal lengths, and check its sides and angles.
Students use the square's properties to explain why PS must be 6 cm and why RS, the angle at R and the angle at S are fixed once PQ and two perpendiculars are drawn.
Students carry out each step of a square or rectangle construction on the stepper tool, choosing the ruler, protractor or compass action, and check the finished figure.
Students explain why a four-sided figure with all angles 90° cannot have unequal opposite sides, by using the equal distance between two perpendiculars.
Students construct rectangles of 4 cm by 6 cm and 2 cm by 10 cm with a ruler and a set square or compass, and check both rectangle properties.
Students construct a rectangle with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, place X on AD and Y on BC, and predict where X and Y are closest and where they are farthest.
Students measure XY for chosen positions of X and Y and record each case as a row of a table with the distance of X from A, the distance of Y from B and the length XY.
Students show that equal distances of X from A and of Y from B give XY equal to AB and ABYX a rectangle, and that the farthest XY is a diagonal of the rectangle.
Students drag X and Y along two opposite sides of a rectangle on the tool, read the length XY, and find the nearest and the farthest positions for different rectangles.
Students draw a rough diagram of a rectangle ACDF made of squares ABEF and BCDE, name the equal sides, and construct it for AF = 4 cm.
Students construct a rectangle that divides into three identical squares by repeating one compass length along a line, and give its sides.
Students give sides of a rectangle that cannot be split into two identical squares and of one that cannot be split into three, using the length-to-breadth test.
Students construct an 8 cm by 4 cm rectangle with a square drawn inside it that shares its centre, using a rough diagram to find the side and the gaps.
Students locate the centre of a square as the meeting point of its two diagonals and use it as the compass tip for a circular hole in the middle.
Students plan and construct a staircase, a shading, a hole and a curve built from squares, circles and arcs, using a rough diagram to choose lengths and tip positions.
Students predict, construct and measure to show that the two diagonals of a rectangle are equal in length.
Students measure the two angles a diagonal makes at a corner, show that they add up to 90°, and name the pairs of equal angles formed by both diagonals.
Students change the sides of a rectangle on the tool, read both diagonals and the angles they make with the sides, and describe what stays the same.
Students explain that the diagonal splits a corner into equal parts only when two adjacent sides are equal, so the rectangle is a square.
Students show that in a square the two diagonals are equal and all eight angles formed with the sides are 45°.
Students state the laws of sides, angles and diagonals of a rectangle and explain why measuring a few rectangles cannot prove a law for all rectangles.
Students construct a rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC splits the corner A into 60° and 30°, using the fact that the two angles add up to 90°.
Students construct rectangles whose diagonal splits a corner into 50° and 40°, and into 45° and 45°, and say what the second one shows about the sides.
Students plan the order of steps for a rectangle with a side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm, and decide which line to draw first.
Students use a circle or an arc of radius 7 cm centred at D to find the point B on the line l, and explain why only a short arc is needed.
Students complete the rectangle with perpendiculars at D and B, and check that opposite sides are equal and every angle is 90°.
Students build a rectangle from a side and a diagonal on the tool, and read the second side that comes out.
Students show that a point where two circles of radius 5 cm meet is 5 cm from both centres, and say why short arcs are enough.
Students construct the house with sides of 5 cm, finding the apex with two arcs and drawing the curved top from the apex.
Students place two points on the tool, set a radius, and watch where the two arcs cross to locate the point at that distance from both, then build a bigger house.
Students construct a four-sided figure with all sides 5 cm and an angle other than 90°, by finding the fourth corner with two arcs.
Students decide whether an equal-sided figure must be a square, construct one that is not, and recreate the Person, Wavy Wave and Eyes artwork with arcs.
Students restate that a circle is all points at one distance from its centre, how a rough diagram plans a construction, and how a rectangle is built from sides or from a side and a diagonal.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Look at five artwork pictures: two circles of the same size side by side and touching; two circles one inside the other with the same centre (the inner one about half the size of the outer); three equal circles in a row, each overlapping the next; a mouse face (one big circle for the face, two smaller circles for the ears, two small circles with dots for the eyes, a dot for the nose and a short line for the mouth); and two lines crossing like an X with a small circle at the bottom end of each line. Try drawing them freehand.
Book item: Mark a point P in your notebook. Then mark as many points as possible, in different directions, that are 4 cm away from P.
Book item: Imagine marking all the points that are 4 cm away from the point P. How would they look?
Book item: How can a compass be used to mark points that are 4 cm from P?
Book item: Take a point on the circle drawn with centre P and radius 4 cm. Is its distance from P equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? What about any other point on the circle?

Book item: Using a ruler and a compass, recreate the artwork pictures: two touching circles, two circles with the same centre, three overlapping circles, the mouse face, and the X with two small circles. Try to make them look as good as the book's pictures.

Book item: Construct this wave: a central straight line AB = 8 cm. The first wave is a half circle on the left half of AB lying above the line (A to X), and the second wave is a half circle on the right half lying below the line (X to B). Both half circles are shaded with vertical lines.

Book item: In the wave with a central line AB = 8 cm, the first wave is a half circle from A to X on the line AB. What radius should be taken in the compass to get this half circle? What should be the length of AX? a) What radius should be taken in the compass? b) What should be the length of AX?
Book item: Take a central line of a different length and try to draw the wave on it.

Book item: Draw a person made of a circle for the head, a short straight neck line below it, and a body that is a rectangle whose top edge is a curved arc dipping in the middle. How will you draw the curved top of the body with a compass? Where should the tip be placed and what radius should be used?

Book item: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.

Book item: Try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half circle (as appearing in the neck of the figure 'A Person'). The challenge here is to get both the waves to be identical. This may be tricky!
Book item: What shapes are a rectangle and four small squares drawn in a group? What makes them squares and rectangles?

Book item: A rectangle ABCD has corners A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). Besides ABCD it can be named BCDA, CDAB, DABC, ADCB, DCBA, CBAD and BADC. Can a rectangle be named using any combination of the labels around its corners? What names are allowed and what names are not?

Book item: Which of the following is not a name for this square? The square has corners S (top left), P (top right), Q (bottom right) and R (bottom left). 1. PQSR 2. SPQR 3. RSPQ 4. QRSP 1) PQSR 2) SPQR 3) RSPQ 4) QRSP

Book item: Identify if there are any squares in this collection. Use measurements if needed. On a dot grid there are four tilted 4-sided figures with corners on dots: A is a diamond whose left to right span equals its top to bottom span (about 8 dots each way); B is a diamond about 6 dots wide and 8 dots tall; C is a diamond about 10 dots wide and 8 dots tall; D is a small tilted long rectangle.

Book item: A square piece of paper has all its sides equal and all angles 90°. It is rotated (tilted so it looks like a diamond). Is it still a square? Are all the sides still equal? Are all the angles still 90°?

Book item: Is it possible to reason out if the sides are equal or not, and if the angles are right or not, without using any measuring instruments in the above figure? Can we do this by only looking at the position of corners in the dot grid?

Book item: Draw the rectangle and four squares configuration (a rectangle in the middle, about twice as wide as tall, with four equal small squares placed near its four corners, one outside each corner, not touching it) on a dot paper. What did you do to recreate this figure so that the four squares are placed symmetrically around the rectangle? Discuss with your classmates.

Book item: Draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid. Draw them such that their corners are on the dots. Verify if the squares and rectangles that you have drawn satisfy their respective properties.
Book item: How would you construct a square with a side of 6 cm? A square PQRS of side length 6 cm is constructed.
Book item: In the construction of square PQRS with PQ = 6 cm, can you see why PS should be 6 cm long?
Book item: In the square PQRS of side 6 cm just constructed, how long is the side RS and what are the measures of ∠R and ∠S?
Book item: Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all the angles are equal to 90° but opposite sides are not equal?
Book item: Draw a rectangle with sides of length 4 cm and 6 cm. After drawing, check if it satisfies both the rectangle properties.
Book item: Draw a rectangle of sides 2 cm and 10 cm. After drawing, check if it satisfies both the rectangle properties.
Book item: Construct a rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.

Book item: In rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, X moves along side AD and Y moves along side BC. At which positions will the points X and Y be at their closest? When do you think they will be the farthest? What does your intuition say? Discuss with your classmates.
Book item: How does the minimum distance between the points X and Y compare to the length of AB (7 cm)?

Book item: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm. Measure XY and fill in: When X is 5 mm away from A and Y is 3 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 1 cm away from A and Y is 1 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 2 cm away from A and Y is 4 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. a) X is 5 mm from A and Y is 3 cm from B b) X is 1 cm from A and Y is 1 cm from B c) X is 2 cm from A and Y is 4 cm from B

Book item: Is there a shorthand way of writing it down? In all the sentences, only the position of X, Y and the length XY changes. So we could write this as a table with columns: Distance of X from A, Distance of Y from B, Length of XY. Fill the table for the three cases above. 1) X from A: 5 mm, Y from B: 3 cm 2) X from A: 1 cm, Y from B: 1 cm 3) X from A: 2 cm, Y from B: 4 cm

Book item: What happens to the length XY when X and Y are placed at the same distance away from A and B, respectively? Fill the table: X from A is 5 mm and Y from B is 5 mm; X from A is 1 cm and Y from B is 1 cm; X from A is 1 cm 5 mm and Y from B is 1 cm 5 mm. 1) 5 mm and 5 mm 2) 1 cm and 1 cm 3) 1 cm 5 mm and 1 cm 5 mm

Book item: In each of these cases (X and Y at the same distance from A and B), observe 1. how the length XY compares to that of AB and 2. the shape of the 4-sided figure ABYX. 1) How XY compares with AB 2) Shape of ABYX
Book item: How does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of AC? BD? (AC and BD are the diagonals of rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.)
Book item: Construct a rectangle ACDF that can be divided into two identical squares ABEF and BCDE, with no measurements imposed. If AF is assigned 4 cm, what must the length of AC be?
Book item: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into 3 identical squares (a rectangle split by two vertical lines into three equal squares).

Book item: Give the lengths of the sides of a rectangle that cannot be divided into two identical squares, and of a rectangle that cannot be divided into three identical squares. a) Cannot be divided into two identical squares b) Cannot be divided into three identical squares

Book item: Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm. How will you construct a square inside, as shown in the figure, such that the centre of the square is the same as the centre of the rectangle? (The square touches the top and bottom of the rectangle and sits in the middle of its length.)
Book item: Construct a square with a circular hole whose centre is the same as the centre of the square.

Book item: Construct three squares of side 4 cm placed in a staircase, each touching the next at one corner (the top right corner of a lower square touches the bottom left corner of the square above it). Now try with squares of side 7 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm placed in the same way, with the 7 cm square at the bottom left and the 3 cm square at the top right.

Book item: Construct the figure: a large square divided into smaller squares, some halved by diagonals with one half shaded with parallel lines, and a plain larger square in a corner. Choose measurements of your choice. The larger 4-sided figure is a square and so are the smaller ones.
Book item: Construct a large square divided into 4 equal smaller squares (2 by 2) with a circular hole in the centre of each small square.

Book item: This is a square with 8 cm sidelengths. Construct it so that four arcs, one on each side, bulge uniformly inwards from each side, each arc going from one corner of its side to the other corner.

Book item: Rectangle PQRS has diagonals PR and QS. Predict whether the two diagonals are equal in length, then construct a rectangle (for example 6 cm by 4 cm) and measure both diagonals. What do you find?

Book item: In rectangle PQRS the diagonal PR divides angle R into g and h, and divides angle P into c and d. Predict, then measure: are g and h equal? Are c and d equal? a) Are g and h equal? b) Are c and d equal?

Book item: In rectangle PQRS, with both diagonals drawn, the eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h (at P: c and d; at Q: e and f; at R: g and h; at S: a and b; c is next to side PS, d next to PQ, e next to QP, f next to QR, g next to RQ, h next to RS, a next to SR, b next to SP). Measure them. Which angles are equal?
Book item: How should the rectangle be constructed so that the diagonal divides the opposite angles into equal parts?

Book item: In your experiment, consider the case when all four sides of the rectangle are equal, that is, a square. Draw a square (for example with side 5 cm), draw both diagonals, and see what happens.
Book item: What general laws did you observe with respect to the angles and sides of a rectangle and its diagonals? Try to frame them.
Book item: How can one be sure that the laws you have observed will always be true?
Book item: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 60° and 30°.
Book item: Angle A of the rectangle is divided by the diagonal into two angles. One measures 60°. Check what the other angle is.
Book item: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 50° and 40°.

Book item: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°. What do you observe about the sides? a) Construct the rectangle. b) What do you observe about the sides?
Book item: Construct a rectangle where one of its sides is 5 cm and the length of a diagonal is 7 cm.
Book item: To construct the rectangle with a side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm, which line can be drawn first?
Book item: Line l is perpendicular to DC at C, and the point B must lie on l. What else do we know about the position of B?
Book item: A circle of radius 7 cm is drawn with centre D, and it meets line l at a point. What is the distance of that point from D?
Book item: In the finished rectangle ABCD (DC = 5 cm, diagonal DB = 7 cm), check that it satisfies R1 (opposite sides are equal in length) and R2 (all the angles are 90°).
Book item: Construct a rectangle one of whose sides is 4 cm and the diagonal is of length 8 cm.
Book item: Construct a rectangle one of whose sides is 3 cm and the diagonal is of length 7 cm.
Book item: The two circles of radius 5 cm centred at B and at C meet at a point (the apex A). How far is that point from B? How far is it from C? a) Distance from B b) Distance from C
Book item: Was it necessary to draw two full circles to get the point A?

Book item: Recreate this house figure. All the lines forming the border of the house are of length 5 cm. The house has a rectangular part with base DE = 5 cm and vertical sides DB = 5 cm and EC = 5 cm, a door 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall on the base, a roof with sides AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm meeting at the top point A, and a curved arc from B to C.
Book item: Construct a bigger house in which all the sides are of length 7 cm.
Book item: Try to recreate ‘A Person’, ‘Wavy Wave’, and ‘Eyes’ from the section ‘Artwork’, using ideas involved in the ‘House’ construction.

Book item: Is there a 4-sided figure in which all the sides are equal in length but is not a square? If such a figure exists, can you construct it? a) Does such a figure exist? b) Can you construct it?

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. A compass keeps one distance fixed, so circles and arcs give exact lengths; squares and rectangles are then built from their properties, and the same two ideas, perpendiculars and arcs, find every corner.

points.text: Each construction starts from a rough diagram and a prediction, then the steps are carried out and checked with a ruler and a protractor.
points.title: Draw, then reason

points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's examples, one tool to do it by hand where the manipulation is the idea, then the book's construction questions in a practice topic.
points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic

points.text: A square and a rectangle have fixed properties, so we measure only what is needed and the properties give the remaining sides and angles.
points.title: Properties do the work

points.text: Wrong ideas such as 'a square is not a rectangle' or 'a diagonal always splits a corner into two equal angles' are raised by Keeko and fixed with a drawing, never just a rule.
points.title: Keeko's doubts
